summary: Specifies the encapsulation of IP and other network layer protocols over X.25 networks, in line with ISO/IEC and CCITT standards, and replaces an earlier RFC for IP over X.25. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: X.25 is an old network that works like phone calls for data. This document explains how to carry Internet packets across it in a standard way.

questions: how is ip sent over x.25
what is null encapsulation in x.25
what is the ip mtu over x.25
subtitle: How IP and other network protocols ride on X.25 virtual circuits, and on ISDN in the packet mode.

tldr.problem: RFC 877 had ambiguities about IP datagram size, X.25 packet size and virtual circuit handling, and gave no interoperable way to carry protocols other than IP between multiprotocol routers and bridges.
tldr.mechanism: The first octet of the X.25 Call User Data field names the protocol (a Network Layer Protocol Identifier), and a Null encapsulation lets one circuit carry many protocols, each PDU starting with its own identifier.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 877, raises the allowed IP MTU from 576 to 1600, and also covers ISDN in the packet mode.

today: RFC 1356 is listed as a Draft Standard and obsoletes RFC 877; the metadata records no later RFC replacing it. Its main change to IP encapsulation is the larger allowed MTU, 1600 instead of 576.

sections.title: Why RFC 877 Needed a Replacement
sections.content:
RFC 877 documented how CSNET and the VAN Gateway sent IP datagrams over X.25 networks. It was widely used, and its IP protocol identifier was included in ISO/IEC TR 9577. RFC 1356 replaces it to fix ambiguities, to align with ISO/IEC standards written afterwards, to allow interoperable multiprotocol operation between routers and bridges, and to add remarks from about 8 years of practical experience.

The inadequacies were in IP datagram MTU size, X.25 maximum data packet size, virtual circuit management and carrying protocols other than IP. As before, X.25 virtual circuits are opened on demand when datagrams arrive and closed after a period of inactivity. The memo also covers the packet mode of ISDN, and ISDN circuit mode only when the circuit is set up as an end-to-end X.25 connection.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook for sending Internet data over the X.25 phone-style network had gaps. This new one fills the gaps and lets more kinds of data share the line.

sections.title: Identifying the Protocol at Call Setup
sections.content:
Messages (PDUs) are sent as X.25 complete packet sequences: each PDU starts on a data packet boundary and the M bit (more data) splits larger PDUs. For IP, the PDU is the IP datagram.

The first octet of the Call User Data (CUD) field in the Call Request is a one-octet NLPID, following ISO/IEC TR 9577, that names the protocol on the circuit. Receivers must ignore any extra octets in the field. Supporting IP is required for conformance.

A system must accept only calls for protocols it can process, and every Internet system must accept the CC encapsulation for IP. It must not accept a call and then immediately clear it: accepting tells the caller the encapsulation is supported, and some networks charge for a call that was accepted and cleared. Support for NLPIDs other than IP should be configurable per peer, while IP (hex CC) must always be allowed between peers.
sections.eli5: When you start the call, the first thing you say is a code word that tells the other side what language you will speak. They only pick up if they know that language.

sections.title: Null Encapsulation and Choices for IP
sections.content:
The single-protocol encodings allow one network protocol per circuit. The Null encapsulation (NLPID hex 00) multiplexes several protocols over one circuit: each complete packet sequence then begins with its own one-octet NLPID, and the protocol may differ from one sequence to the next. A receiver that supports Null encapsulation for any protocol must accept the call, and may silently discard PDUs for protocols it cannot handle. This is the method most likely to be used by a multiprotocol router to avoid using too many virtual circuits. Using IEEE 802.1d bridging across X.25 requires the Null encapsulation.

Single-protocol circuits use bandwidth more efficiently when few protocols are involved, let each side know exactly which protocols its partner supports, and allow per-protocol accounting and different quality of service or window sizes.

By default, IP datagrams must be sent on a circuit opened with the CC CUD, to stay compatible with RFC 877 systems. Implementations may also support IP in multiplexed packets, in SNAP encapsulation (OUI 00-00-00, PID 08-00), or in SNAP inside multiplexed packets. If any of these is supported, the implementation must accept it, and must allow the sending encapsulation to be configured per peer address.
sections.eli5: You can have one phone line per language, or one line where each sentence starts with a tag saying which language it is in. The second saves lines but needs more tagging.

sections.title: Packet Sizes and the IP MTU
sections.content:
Any maximum X.25 data packet size may be configured or negotiated, and there is no implied link between PDU size and X.25 packet size. The RFC 877 method of setting the IP MTU from the X.25 packet size is no longer used.

Every system must be able to receive and transmit PDUs of at least 1600 octets. The default transmit MTU for IP should be 1500 and must be configurable in at least the range 576 to 1600. Being able to send with an MTU of 576 and receive datagrams of 1600 is essential to interoperate with RFC 877 implementations. On a Null-encapsulated circuit the extra identifier octet matters: with the CC identifier an MTU of 1500 means a PDU of 1501, and with a SNAP header for IP it means 1506.

The remarks add that bigger X.25 packets do not always mean better performance. Many X.25 networks store each packet fully in every switch, so large packets over slow trunks can add delay, and sending a datagram as a sequence of smaller packets allows more pipelining.
sections.eli5: Big boxes are not always faster, because every stop on the road has to unload the whole box. Sending a few smaller boxes can get the goods there sooner.

sections.title: Managing Virtual Circuits
sections.content:
Each ISO/IEC TR 9577 encapsulation needs its own virtual circuit between two systems, and several circuits may be opened for one encapsulation, for example to raise throughput. Receivers should accept multiple incoming calls with the same encapsulation, and must not accept a call only to close it or ignore its PDUs. Because multiple circuits are allowed, call collision prevention algorithms must not be implemented.

Either side may close a circuit, and a datagram being sent when it closes is lost. Every system must use an inactivity timer to clear idle circuits, because some networks, including the ISDN at the time, charge for holding time. The timer should be configurable and its default a small number of minutes; for IP, 90 seconds is called reasonable. Systems should also use a configurable hold-down timer so calls to failed destinations are not retried immediately.

On the X.25 features side, call setup and clearing and complete packet sequences are mandatory. Interrupt packets and the Q bit must not be used, and the D bit modification facility must not be subscribed because it interferes with the M bit. Clearing an unsupported call may use diagnostic code 249 (ISO/IEC 8208 systems) or 0.
sections.eli5: Phone-style connections cost money while they are open, so each side hangs up when nothing is being said for a while and waits a bit before redialing a number that did not answer.

sections.title: Operational Remarks and Address Resolution
sections.content:
The general remarks are guidelines drawn from experience with RFC 877, not requirements. Protocols above the network layer, such as TCP, do not affect the standard, and no circuit is opened per TCP connection. Some X.25 implementations hand CC calls to the X.29 PAD (remote login) facility when IP is not running; a caller can detect this if it receives data packets with the Q bit set, and should then clear the call and log the problem.

Opening multiple circuits to one destination may help when the X.25 window is the limit, but it takes a bigger share of the shared path, can reorder datagrams and may raise cost.

The RFC specifies no method of dynamic IP to X.25 (X.121) address resolution and leaves it for further study. Typical implementations use static tables or an algorithmic transformation, and DNS resource records from RFC 1183 are described as entirely experimental.
sections.eli5: The authors add friendly tips from experience, such as what to do when the wrong person answers the phone. The document does not say how to look up phone numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. Nothing in the protocol description adds authentication or protection of the data carried.
sections.eli5: The document does not say how to keep the calls private. It only explains how to set up and label them.

items.desc: Decimal 128; five-octet SNAP header follows in the call request.

items.desc: Decimal 0; multiplexes several protocols over one circuit.
